recent_posts.title: PPI data is out
recent_posts.body:
BREAKING: US PPI YOY ACTUAL 5.4% (FORECAST 5.3%, PREVIOUS 4.7%)

The producer price index, a measure of final-demand costs for goods and services, increased a seasonally adjusted 0.4% for the month, in line with the Dow Jones consensus, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Thursday.

On an annual basis, that put PPI at 5.4%, still well above the Fed’s 2% inflation target and 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. PPI rose 0.1% in July, a slight upward revision from the original estimate of no change.

Excluding food and energy, core PPI accelerated by 0.2%, against the forecast for a 0.3% increase. Core less trade services, another volatile category, was up 0.3%.

Stock market futures were negative following the report, the release of which coincided with U.S. crude oil prices topping $100 a barrel. Treasury yields moved sharply higher.

Energy prices in particular and goods prices overall were responsible for most of the increase. Final-demand energy prices rose 4.2%, pushed largely by soaring diesel, which surged 24.1%. Goods prices broadly increased 1.1%.

Services prices were up just 0.1%, with a 2.3% increase in transportation and warehousing accounting for much of that move.

My Greatest Edge in the Market Is Knowing How to Wait (Long Read)
recent_posts.body:
I Don’t Chase the Market. I Make the Market Earn My Capital.

https://afterhour.com/Legitimate_Risk/bvPF/if-theres-one-thing-youd-like-

Most people think making money in the market requires constantly doing something.

Buying. Selling. Finding the next stock. Reacting to every red candle. Chasing every green one.

I approach the market differently.

A large part of my strategy is doing absolutely nothing.

That doesn't mean I'm not paying attention. It means I've learned that activity and productivity are not the same thing in the stock market.

Sometimes the most profitable decision I can make is to sit in cash and wait.

I Don't Chase Green

One of my simplest rules is that I generally don't buy on green days.

If something I like suddenly runs 5%, 8%, or 10%, my instinct isn't:

"I better get in before I miss it."

It's usually:

"Good. Now I'll wait."

Maybe the stock pulls back next week. Maybe another company becomes more attractive. Maybe the entire market gives me a better opportunity.

And if none of that happens?

I missed a stock.

That's it.

Missing a winner costs me nothing. Chasing one at the wrong price can cost me real money.

Cash Is a Position

I don't feel pressure to keep every dollar invested.

Cash gives me optionality.

When everyone else is panicking during a selloff, I don't want to discover that all my capital is already deployed. I want buying power.

I'm willing to wait days, weeks, or longer if the opportunities in front of me don't offer the odds I want.

My money doesn't have an expiration date.

The Market Doesn't Pay Me for Being Busy

The market doesn't care how many trades I make or how many hours I spend staring at charts.

It rewards good decisions and punishes bad ones.

So before I deploy capital, I ask:

Are the odds actually in my favor?

My general minimum is around 60/40.

When I'm evaluating a company, I also want the potential reward to justify the downside I'm accepting. Ideally, I'm looking for approximately 2:1 reward-to-risk, with meaningful separation between potential upside and downside.

If the numbers aren't there, I don't force the trade.

I wait.

A Great Company Can Still Be a Bad Trade

I can love a company and still refuse to buy its stock.

If the price has already exploded upward, I don't chase it simply because I believe in the business.

A great company can still be a bad trade at the wrong price.

I'd rather wait for a normal 5% to 10% pullback and reevaluate.

And if a stock suddenly drops more than 10% in one session, I don't automatically assume it's on sale either. I want to understand why it dropped and give the price time to stabilize.

Green doesn't make me chase.

Red doesn't make me buy.

Price alone doesn't make the decision.

Patience Doesn't Mean Stubbornness

Once I own something, I give my thesis time to work.

I'm generally thinking in 12-to-18-month windows, not tomorrow afternoon.

But patience doesn't mean blindly holding forever.

If fundamentals deteriorate, the thesis changes, or new information changes the probabilities, I reevaluate.

Ordinary volatility isn't enough to scare me out of a position, just as a rising price isn't enough to convince me I was right.

The thesis matters more than today's candle.

I Let Winners Earn More Capital

This is where my approach is almost backward compared with many retail investors.

People will watch a stock fall 30% and immediately buy more. Then they'll watch another stock rise 30% and sell because they're afraid of losing the profit.

I prefer making the company prove itself.

If one of my positions rises 30% to 40%, fundamentals remain strong, volume confirms the move, institutional interest increases, and my forward thesis still supports more upside, I may add more.

That's why I prefer averaging up to automatically averaging down.

Strength earns more of my money. Weakness doesn't.

There are exceptions when I average down, but even then I don't turn it into a desperate double-or-nothing bet.

If a $1,000 starter position falls 40% and is now worth roughly $600, I might add around $400 if I've rerun the thesis and the reward-to-risk still meets my criteria.

I'm restoring the allocation, not gambling twice as much because the market disagreed with me.

Patience Is Risk Management

To me, patience isn't just a personality trait.

It's risk management.

Waiting prevents me from chasing.

It keeps cash available.

It gives me time to gather information.

It allows a falling stock to show whether it's experiencing a temporary correction or something fundamentally worse.

And it gives good companies enough time for the thesis to develop.

Waiting costs me nothing. Being wrong with money already deployed does.

There will always be another earnings season, another correction, another panic, another opportunity.

I don't need all of them.

I need the ones where the probabilities favor me.

My Patience Checklist

Before I deploy more capital, I want to be able to answer:

✅ Do I understand what I'm buying?

✅ Do I understand why I'm buying it?

✅ Is the potential reward worth the downside?

✅ Are the odds approximately 60/40 or better?

✅ Is the reward-to-risk attractive enough?

✅ Am I buying because of my thesis rather than FOMO?

✅ Am I comfortable giving the thesis 12 to 18 months?

If I can't answer those questions comfortably, I can wait.

The Bottom Line

I research first.

I establish my bull case.

I establish my bear case.

I calculate what I could potentially make and what I could potentially lose.

Then I decide whether the market deserves my money.

Sometimes it does.

Sometimes it doesn't.

Sometimes I'll watch a stock run without me.

That's fine.

My goal was never to catch every winner.

My goal is to survive every cycle, protect my capital, compound my winners, and repeatedly put money behind favorable probabilities.

Missing an opportunity doesn't hurt my portfolio. Forcing one can.

The market can move as fast as it wants.

I don't chase the market. I make the market earn my capital.

TL;DR

My patience is simple: I don't trade because the market is moving. I trade when the odds, price, fundamentals, and reward-to-risk justify putting my capital at risk.

Cash is a position. Missing a stock is acceptable. Chasing isn't. And when a company proves my thesis right, I'm willing to give the winner more capital.

CRWV: Explosive AI Growth With an Explosive Balance Sheet

CoreWeave (CRWV) is one of the purest ways to invest in AI infrastructure. Q2 2026 revenue reached $2.58 billion, but the company still lost $626 million. Demand for its GPU cloud infrastructure remains enormous, but CoreWeave requires staggering amounts of capital to build the data centers and computing capacity needed to satisfy that demand. 

At roughly $100 today, CRWV easily clears our $10B market-cap requirement at around $50B+. Wall Street remains bullish but unusually divided: Yahoo shows an average target of $144.46, with estimates ranging all the way from $39 to $317. Recent targets include Truist at $165, Citi at $159, Wells Fargo at $160 and Cantor at $176. 

The problem is risk. CoreWeave's heavy debt load and capital requirements are significant enough that its five-year credit-default swaps recently traded above 800 basis points, signaling serious credit concerns. 

My 12–18 month range: Bull $175–$200 | Bear $50–$65. Using ~$100 as our starting point, the midpoint gives roughly 88% upside versus 43% downside, or about 2.0:1. So CRWV barely passes our 2:1 screen, but I'd put it in the high-risk category. The upside is exceptional if AI demand and execution continue, but unlike ORCL, the balance sheet gives us very little room for mistakes.

recent_posts.title: Why is AfterHour in a State of Decline
recent_posts.body:
Are you sad watching this app die a slow death? Same. Let’s fix it. 

Everyone’s answer as to the reason for the decline is the same: @SirJack checked out, the bugs never got fixed, no new features. Some will even mention the Great AH Coin Rug Pull of ‘25. I don’t buy these reasons as the primary cause. I think they are easy excuses.

Communities tolerate absurd amounts of jank when they’re getting value. Twitter fell over weekly for years and people kept posting. Reddit’s interface was actively hostile for a decade and it became the front page of the internet anyway. Nobody leaves a room they want to be in because the door sticks. When people start citing the product, they’ve usually already left emotionally and are reaching for a reason that doesn’t cost them anything to say out loud.

Here’s what I think is actually going on.

It’s harder to hide a bad call here. On X you post a thesis, it blows up, you scroll past it and post something else. The feed is a firehose and nobody’s keeping score (unless you’re Kevin Xu and then everybody on X is tracking every call you make 😂).
But here it’s a small room and people remember. Your bad call sits in the same feed as everyone who watched you make it. So when shit turns south, it’s hard to own it, to remind everyone that you “fucked up.” Silence gets built into every drawdown, and that’s a feature of a small, accountable community. 

The best posters graduate. You build an audience here, then take it somewhere you can monetize it. Substack, X, wherever. Without a way to keep that value on-platform, this is a farm system, and the top decile is permanently walking out the door. Right, @SIRJACK? 

Thesis exhaustion. We talk a lot about the same handful of tickers through discovery → crowd → catalyst → resolution. After resolution there’s nothing left to say. If new ideas aren’t entering the funnel, the feed stagnates. 

And then reverse Metcalfe does the rest. Network value scales with the square of participants, which means it falls that way too. You post, get one reply instead of four, and you feel like you’re shouting into a canyon. So you post less. But your posts were generating someone else’s replies, so their density drops too, and around it goes. The decline overshoots whatever triggered it by a mile, and then gets blamed on whatever’s most visible. Usually the product.

So fix the loop, not the app.
1. Post your losers. The drawdown posts are worth ten times the victory laps and most people don’t post them. 
2. Comment density is the whole ballgame and it’s the one input we fully control. 
3. Bring a name nobody here is talking about instead of the eleventh take on the same ticker.
4. When someone new posts a real thesis, engage with it like it matters, because that’s the difference between them coming back tomorrow and not.

This app is merely the wrapper, not the product. We are the product. Our content, our replies, our likes. This app doesn’t exist without our engagement. So let’s fix the product we can actually control, ourselves. 

*steps off soap box*

recent_posts.title: $ONDS Q2 Earnings Report Card
recent_posts.body:
Four things matter for $ONDS earnings. Ignore the rest. 

1. Revenue - Grade: A
$83.8M vs ~$68M consensus. Up 67% sequentially, 13x year over year, 85% organic on a same-portfolio basis. Raised the year to $525-550M, guided Q3 to $140-155M. You don’t guide up after a bad quarter.

2. Margin - Grade: A-
Adjusted gross margin 50.4% vs 51.5% in Q1. Flat while volume grew two-thirds, incremental margin around 49%. That answers a big question: does the backlog convert at decent economics? It does. The 43.1% in the headlines is intellectual property amortization running through cost of goods sold. Non-cash. Ignore. 

3. Growth - Grade: A
Backlog $613M reported, $757M pro forma, from $68M at year end 2025. $175M in new orders during Q2, another $105M already captured in Q3. Best part of this release. 

4. Cash Burn - Grade: C
Adjusted cash operating expense went $36.9M to $93.2M. Adjusted EBITDA loss $50.6M vs $10.9M. Q2 was guided as the peak loss quarter and it was. Street had cash opex near $50-55M and that got nearly doubled. Most of the increase looks like acquired cost from acquisitions rather than new spend. 10-Q may help answer this. 

I could see a grade below C based on the numbers but because they pulled profitability guidance forward while printing their worst burn quarter, I think a C is appropriate. Nobody does that with loose costs. 

Overall: B+. 
Three of four areas did about as well as they could. The fourth is a fair concern and we’ll find out next quarter if it is a real issue. Watch adjusted cash opex in Q3 earnings to validate. 

If we take midpoint of Q3 revenue range at $147M and with 50% margin you clear roughly $73M of gross profit. Opex flat near $93M in Q3 means the spend was front-loaded as Eric stated and if that happens then Q4 profitability is certainly in play. If opex isn’t flat, we’ll need correspondingly higher revenue than what was guided.

recent_posts.title: When should you buy to close an option?
recent_posts.body:
Time to learn ya something while the market is closed.

The usual rule of thumb is to consider closing when you’ve captured more than 50% of the premium before 50% of the time has passed. But what happens when you capture a smaller profit extremely quickly? 
I recently sold three $APP $300 cash-secured puts with 293 days until expiration for $62 per share, collecting $18,600 in premium. 
The next day, $APP jumped roughly 10%, and I bought the puts back for $55. That locked in a $2,100 profit after holding the trade for only one day.

I captured just 11.29% of the available premium, but only 0.34% of the original time had elapsed.

That led me to create the Trade Efficiency Ratio:
* η = % of premium captured ÷ % of time elapsed

For this trade, η was 33.2. I captured premium roughly 33 times faster than time was passing... Which is pretty dang efficient despite only being 11% of the premium realized.

I wrote a full article explaining how I’m using this ratio to help decide when to buy options back early. Link in the comments.

recent_posts.title: $JD at $27.90
recent_posts.body:
$39.9B market cap. $32.8B in cash and short-term investments at the end of Q2. Back the balance sheet out and you're paying roughly $23B for a business doing $191B in revenue.

The reason it's cheap: Aug 13 they posted the first revenue decline since the 2014 IPO, -2.9%. Stock fell 8%.

Same quarter, though : non-GAAP net income +20.8%, operating income swung from a loss to RMB 4.5B, EPS beat by 12%, and revenue actually beat consensus too.

The honest bear case, because it's a good one: ~91% of that operating improvement came from cutting food-delivery losses, not from growth. You only stop burning money once. And JD lost that war : ~16M daily orders vs Meituan's 80M.

What keeps me interested is the capital return. ~17% of shares retired since 2023. 3.6% dividend. ~6.9% total shareholder yield. At that pace revenue doesn't need to grow, it needs to stop falling.

Breaks if revenue hasn't turned by mid-2027.

Started writing these up properly : full piece here: https://rm20252029.substack.com/p/the-market-is-pricing-jdcom-like

Not financial advice.

recent_posts.title: Patience is a skill, not a personality trait
recent_posts.body:
Day 5/31 of free content. 

——

People talk about patience the way they talk about height. You either have it or you do not. Some people are just calm. Some are wired hot. Draw of the genetic lottery, nothing to be done, better find a strategy that suits your temperament.

I think this is one of the more damaging ideas in circulation, and not only because it lets everybody off the hook.

Patience is a capacity, and capacities are built. The reason it looks like a personality trait is that the people who have built it did so somewhere you were not watching, the building took years, and now you see only the finished thing and assume it was standard issue.

**What patience actually is**

The first thing that has to go: patience is not the absence of urgency. It is not calmness. Genuinely patient people are not sitting there serenely unbothered. That is a fantasy, and holding it as the target makes real patience feel like failure, because you will always be able to feel the urgency and conclude you do not have the thing.

**Patience is the ability to feel the urge and not act on it.** The urge is still there. It is loud. You have simply developed the capacity to hold it without discharging it.

That reframe matters enormously, because it turns patience from a state you are supposed to achieve into a muscle you can be observed using. You cannot practice being calm. You can absolutely practice wanting to do the thing and not doing it.

The second thing that has to go: patience is not passivity. Waiting for the right conditions while remaining fully alert is exhausting. It is a much higher-energy activity than doing something. The tiredness of a day spent not trading is real and it surprises people, who expected doing nothing to feel restful. **Vigilance without discharge is work.**

**Why it is so hard, mechanically**

There is a reason waiting is difficult, and it is not weakness.

Your nervous system runs on a very old, very effective rule. An action that resolves discomfort gets reinforced. Feel the itch, scratch it, the itch goes away, you have learned to scratch. This mechanism is why you are alive. Thirst, hunger, fear. The loop is fast, it is physical, and it does not consult you.

Now put a person in front of a screen where something is moving and they have money at stake. The discomfort of watching is real. Taking an action, any action, resolves it immediately, regardless of whether the action was correct. **The relief arrives at the moment of the click, not at the moment of the outcome.** You feel better within a second. You find out whether you were right in three days.

That is a reinforcement loop pointed directly at the wrong behavior. The click gets rewarded on a one-second delay. The correctness gets rewarded on a three-day delay, if at all, and gets tangled up with luck on the way. Your nervous system is going to learn the fast signal. It always does. This is not a character flaw. It is what nervous systems are for.

Which means **willpower is the wrong tool.** Willpower is you, consciously, in real time, arguing against a system that is faster than you and does not use language. You will win that argument sometimes. You will not win it consistently, and the times you lose will cluster, because the argument gets harder exactly when you are tired, or behind, or have already lost once today.

If you have ever wondered why your discipline evaporates specifically on the days it matters most, that is why. You were relying on the resource that depletes.

**How it is actually built**

**1. Make the waiting have a job.**

Undefined waiting is nearly impossible to sustain. "Wait for a good setup" gives your attention nothing to do, so it goes and finds something, and what it finds is usually a reason to act.

Defined waiting is completely different. "I am waiting for this specific condition, and until it appears my job is to check these three things and then look away." Now waiting is an activity with a shape. You can do it badly or well. You can tell whether you are doing it.

This is the same reason a checklist beats a resolution. A resolution asks you to be a certain kind of person. A checklist asks you to do a specific next thing.

**2. Shorten the loop on the right behavior.**

The correct action gets rewarded too slowly. So build a fast reward for it.

Logging a skipped setup with the rule you applied is a tiny, immediate act of self-acknowledgement. You did the right thing and something happened right then, a mark on a page. It sounds too small to matter. It is not. You are inserting a fast signal into a loop that previously had none, and the fast signal is the only kind your nervous system is listening to.

A tally of "times I waited correctly" is worth more to your behavior than a lecture to yourself about discipline, because one of those is a reinforcement mechanism and the other is a speech.

**3. Remove the option instead of resisting it.**

The most patient people I know are not resisting more than you. **They are resisting less, because they have arranged things so the impulsive action is not available.**

Close the trading app. Set the alert and leave the room. Have a written rule that says the position is entered at the open or not at all. Every one of these converts a moment-by-moment willpower expenditure into a single up-front decision made while calm.

There is no honour in white-knuckling it. The person who deleted the app from their phone and the person who has the app and does not open it are not in a contest. The first one has engineered a better environment and will still be doing this in ten years.

**4. Practise it somewhere cheap.**

You cannot learn to hold discomfort in the situation where holding it costs the most. That is like learning to swim in a rip current.

So practise where it is cheap. Sit with an unanswered message for an hour. Let the phone ring out. Order the thing and do not check the tracking. Cook something that takes forty minutes when there is a fifteen-minute option. All of these are reps of the same movement. Feel the urge, do not discharge it, notice you survived.

That last part is the active ingredient. Every rep teaches your nervous system a fact it does not currently believe. **The discomfort goes away on its own.** You do not have to act to make it stop. It stops, if you wait, and the waiting is survivable.

You only learn that by living through it repeatedly. No amount of reading it, including reading it here, installs it.

**The part about life**

I have framed all this around screens and money, because that is the context. But it is not really about that, and pretending otherwise would be a disservice.

The same capacity is what lets you sit with a child who is upset without immediately trying to fix it. It is what lets you not send the reply for a day. It is what lets you stay in a hard conversation past the point where you want to leave the room, and stay in a career or a project or a marriage past the point where it stops being novel.

Almost everything worth having is on the other side of a stretch where nothing appears to be happening. That is a structural feature of good things rather than an obstacle in front of them. Compounding is slow at the start, always, by arithmetic. Skill plateaus before it steps. Relationships have long flat sections that are not a problem to solve.

The people who get the good outcomes are very often not the ones who found a faster path. They are the ones who could tolerate the flat part without needing it to be exciting.

And here is the thing I actually want you to take away. **The flat part is not lost time.** It feels like the interval before the real thing starts. It is most of the thing. If you spend all of it waiting for it to be over, you will have spent most of your life in a waiting room that was, in fact, the destination.

**A modest, achievable version**

I do not want to end with anything grand, because grand resolutions are the enemy here.

Pick one place this week where you habitually reach for the fast resolution. Not the biggest one. A small one. The phone in the queue. The message you answer instantly. The position you check nine times a day.

Do it once fewer than usual. Notice, specifically, that nothing bad happened.

That is a rep. Worth roughly nothing on its own, and roughly everything a thousand times.

**Today's one thing**

Sit for two minutes without your phone. Two. Not meditating, not doing anything, just sitting, with the urge to reach for it fully present.

Time it, because you will want to believe it has been longer than it has. It will be uncomfortable for about ninety seconds and then it will ease on its own, without you doing anything.

That easing, the fact that it happens by itself, is the entire lesson, and you cannot be told it. You have to watch it happen once.

**Tomorrow, a short one: why the scoreboard lies over short periods, and what to look at instead.**

recent_posts.title: Keep a record of the trades you didn't take
recent_posts.body:
Day 4/31 of free content. Keep the trend going

——

Your journal has a hole in it, and the hole is shaped like every decision you made that did not result in a transaction.

If you keep records at all, and most people do not, you record what you did. Entry, exit, size, result, maybe a note about how you felt. Reasonable. That is what a journal is.

Consider what that record can and cannot tell you. It contains only the trades you took. Every trade you considered and passed on is invisible. Every setup you spotted at 10:14 and talked yourself out of by 10:19 has left no trace. Every time you were about to size up and did not, gone.

So when you sit down at the end of the month to work out what you are doing wrong, you are analysing a dataset that has been filtered by the exact process you are trying to evaluate. **The filter is the thing under investigation, and you have thrown away everything it removed.**

This is survivorship bias, running inside your own head, on your own decisions, every day.

**Three kinds of not-trading**

**Type 1. You never saw it.** The setup happened, it would have worked, and you were making coffee. This is a coverage problem rather than a discipline problem. You cannot watch everything and you should not try. Type 1 non-trades are noise and you should feel nothing about them.

**Type 2. You saw it and passed for a reason you can name.** "Spread was too wide." "Earnings tomorrow and I do not hold through earnings." "I already have three positions in the same theme." "Outside my plan."

These are the good ones. A Type 2 non-trade is a win, whether or not the trade would have worked. You applied a rule. The rule cost you money this time and will save you money over a hundred instances. If you only ever record the trades you took, you will never see the accumulated value of these, and your rules will feel like nothing but a source of regret.

**Type 3. You saw it, it was inside your plan, and you did not take it anyway.** No rule was applied. You hesitated. You were still sore from yesterday. You wanted one more confirmation. You went to check one more chart and by the time you came back the price had gone.

This is the only category that is actually a problem, and it is completely invisible in a normal journal.

**Type 3 is where the money is.** Not because the individual missed trades were profitable, sometimes they were not, but because Type 3 is a direct measurement of the gap between your plan and your behaviour, and that gap is the most fixable thing about most traders.

**What it costs you to not see this**

**You blame the strategy for a discipline problem.** Your results are mediocre. The trades in your journal are a mixed bag. So you conclude the strategy is not working and go looking for a new one.

Suppose your plan generated 40 valid setups this month and you took 22, and the 18 you skipped were, as a group, better than the 22 you took. That is an entirely different diagnosis. The strategy is fine. **The strategy has never been tested, because you have never actually run it.** You have been running a version of it filtered through your mood.

People change strategies for years without discovering this, because the evidence needed to discover it is the evidence they never collect.

**You cannot tell whether your rules earn their keep.** You have a rule: no trades in the last 30 minutes. Does it help? No idea. Your journal contains zero late-day trades, that is what the rule does, so there is nothing to evaluate. The rule might be saving you a fortune. It might be costing you your best hour. Both look identical from inside a journal that only records fills.

Log the skips and the rule becomes measurable. After sixty instances you will know, and you can keep it, kill it, or narrow it, based on something other than folklore.

**How to do it without hating your life**

Nobody logs non-trades because it sounds like enormous work. It is not, if you keep it brutally small.

Log only Type 2 and Type 3. Ignore Type 1 entirely. You cannot audit what you never saw.

Four fields.

1. **Ticker and time.**
    
2. **What the setup was**, five words maximum. "Gap fill, held VWAP." Enough to recognise it later.
    
3. **Why you did not take it.** This is the important one, because it forces the Type 2 / Type 3 split. If you can name a rule, write the rule. If you cannot, write "no reason." Those two words, honestly recorded, are worth more than the rest of the journal combined.
    
4. **What happened**, one line at the end of the day. Not to torture yourself. To build the dataset.
    

Ten seconds an entry. Maybe six entries a day. A minute of your life.

Then once a month, count. How many Type 3s? What did they do as a group? That is the review. One number, and it will tell you something your fills never could.

**The trap to avoid**

There is a way to do this badly, and naming it matters because it turns a useful practice into a corrosive one.

Do not use the non-trade log to torture yourself with what you missed. "I would have made $4,000." That number is fictional for three reasons. You would not have sized it the way you are imagining. You would not have held it to the point you are imagining. And you are looking at a completed move that you would have been sitting inside, uncertainly, in real time.

The log is a behavioural instrument. You are counting how often you deviate from your own plan, and in which direction. The individual outcomes barely matter. **The count is the point.**

If you notice yourself feeling sick reading it back, you are using it wrong. Zoom out to the count and stop looking at the rows.

**The reframe worth taking into the weekend**

The best traders I know are not the ones with the best entries. **They are the ones with the smallest gap between what they said they would do and what they actually did.**

That gap is invisible unless you measure it. And you cannot measure it from a record of your fills, because your fills are, by definition, the times the gap was zero.

So start writing down the ones that got away, and much more importantly the ones you let get away on purpose, for a reason you can name. The second group is your discipline, made visible for the first time.

**Today's one thing**

For today only, keep a sticky note next to your screen. Every time you look at something and do not take it, write the ticker and one of two things. The rule, or "no reason."

At the close, count how many say "no reason."

That number is your homework for the weekend. Not to fix. Just to know.

**Tomorrow: patience, and why it is a trainable skill rather than a personality you were or were not born with.**

💵When to Sell: Elaborated Rules & Examples
Here is an in-depth breakdown of the four rules for selling, complete with the real-world and personal examples the author shares in the book.

1. You Made a Mistake

If the initial reason you bought the stock is no longer valid, or if you discover your original thesis was wrong, it is time to cut your losses and move on. Don't let psychological anchoring (the pain of losing money) keep you tied to an invalid investment.

Example: EMC Corporation: In the mid-1990s, the author bought a position in EMC Corporation, a computer storage company, despite it being a bit pricey at 20 times earnings. While the stock soared from $5 to $100 in three years and then crashed back to $5 a year later, the author sold only a third at a high price. The lesson: a great purchase decision can result in a poor overall return if you fail to sell when the price reaches an unsustainable level.

Example: Commercial Movie Projectors: The author bought a manufacturer of commercial movie projectors based on expectations of a multiplex-building boom. The boom waned, and theater owners began struggling with debt and interest payments rather than buying new projectors. Even though it meant taking a loss, the author sold the stock—which was a good move because the shares subsequently plunged to penny-stock levels.

2. Fundamentals Change for the Worse

Even exceptional companies can hit a wall. When a business experiences a permanent shift that hurts its economic moat, it is time to sell. As economist John Maynard Keynes said: "When the facts change, I change my mind."

Example: Getty Images: Getty built a massive, highly profitable database of digital images during photography's digital migration. However, as digital cameras became more accessible and higher-quality imaging became cheaper, web sites began selling lower-quality, much cheaper images (a few dollars versus hundreds). This digital technology made Getty's economic model less relevant and hurt its growth prospects.

3. You Find a Better Place for Your Money

Capital is a finite resource. If you have limited capital, you should constantly look for the highest expected return.

Example: The 2007 Financial Crisis: During the late summer 2007 credit crunch, financial stocks were crushed. The author found themselves with very little cash but noticed bank stocks trading below book value that were already slated to be bought out at higher prices. The author sold a position they hadn't owned very long that only had modest upside potential to fund this more lucrative bank stock purchase.

Alternatively, Cash is King: If a stock surpasses its fundamental value and the expected return turns negative, selling makes sense even if you don't have another investment idea, because earning nothing (cash) is better than a negative return.

4. The Position Becomes Too Large

When a stock has an incredible run, it can grow to represent an uncomfortable percentage of your portfolio.

Example 5: Portfolio Concentration: The author notes that at one point, half of their personal portfolio consisted of just two stocks. However, many investors prefer to limit individual positions to around 5% of their portfolio. If a stock grows to over 10% of your portfolio and makes you anxious ("gives you the willies"), it is entirely reasonable to trim the position to reduce risk to a comfortable level.

💡 The Bottom Line:
None of these four reasons are based on short-term movements in stock prices. The trick is to stay focused on the future value of the business, not the past performance of the shares. Selling simply because the price drops or skyrockets makes no sense unless the actual value of the business has changed in tandem.
